blocks.content: Think about ordering coffee at a cafe. You walk up, say what you want, and wait. You don't grind the beans, steam the milk, or pull the shot yourself, you just ask, and the barista and the espresso machine do the actual work.

Client-server architecture is that same relationship, wearing a computer science hat. One side asks for something, the other side does the work and sends back an answer. Splitting the asker from the doer is one of the oldest and most useful ideas in all of computing, and it's the starting assumption behind almost every system design question you'll ever get asked.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396262051-575713515.png
blocks.alt: A single client sending a request to a single server, which sends back a response

blocks.content: This topic looks simple, and it mostly is, but it's the seed that grows into everything else in this course. Load balancers, horizontal scaling, caching, stateless services, all of that exists because this simple pattern works so well that a single server eventually can't keep up with everyone asking it for things.
1. The core idea: someone asks, someone answers
blocks.text: 1. The core idea: someone asks, someone answers

blocks.content: A client is anything that sends a request. A server is anything that receives a request, does the actual work, and sends back a response. That's the whole pattern. Everything else in system design is detail layered on top of this one idea.
1.1 The client's job: ask and wait
blocks.text: 1.1 The client's job: ask and wait

blocks.content: The client's entire job is to ask for something and know what to do with the answer. It doesn't need to know how the work gets done behind the scenes. Your browser has no idea how Instagram's servers actually build your feed, it just sends a request and renders whatever comes back.
["Sends a request in a format the server understands","Waits for a response, usually with some kind of timeout","Renders or uses whatever comes back, a webpage, a JSON payload, a file"]
items: Sends a request in a format the server understands
Waits for a response, usually with some kind of timeout
Renders or uses whatever comes back, a webpage, a JSON payload, a file

blocks.content: 1.2 The server's job: do the actual work
blocks.text: 1.2 The server's job: do the actual work

blocks.content: The server holds the logic, the data, or both. It listens for requests, figures out what's being asked, does whatever work that requires, reading from a database or running a calculation, and sends the result back. Ask it the same question twice and, unless something changed, you get the same kind of answer both times.

blocks.title: The server doesn't care who's asking
blocks.content: A well built server responds the same way to a browser, a mobile app, or a curl command, as long as the request looks the same. It has no idea, and doesn't need to know, what's on the other end.
2. Why separate the asker from the doer
blocks.text: 2. Why separate the asker from the doer

blocks.content: This split isn't just how things happen to be built, it's genuinely powerful, for a few concrete reasons.
2.1 Clients stay thin and simple

Because the server does the heavy lifting, the client can stay small and simple. It doesn't need a database, it doesn't need business logic, it just needs to know how to send a request and display a response. That's why a browser can run on a phone with a fraction of a server's resources and still do useful work.
2.2 Servers can scale and upgrade independently
blocks.text: 2.2 Servers can scale and upgrade independently

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396262051-185225110.png
blocks.alt: A client staying the same while the server behind it is swapped from an old version to an upgraded one

blocks.content: You can rewrite the entire server, swap its database, change its programming language, or add ten more machines behind it, and the client doesn't notice, as long as the requests and responses look the same. That independence is what lets teams ship improvements constantly without anyone touching the app on your phone.
2.3 Many clients can share one server's logic and data
blocks.text: 2.3 Many clients can share one server's logic and data

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396262052-592297098.png
blocks.alt: Three separate clients all sending requests to the same shared server

blocks.content: One server, or one fleet of servers, can serve thousands or millions of clients at once, all sharing the same logic and the same data. Nobody has to duplicate the server's code on their own device. Everyone just asks, and the same brain answers everyone.

blocks.title: This is what makes updates painless
blocks.content: Fix a bug or ship a new feature on the server, and every client benefits immediately, without anyone installing anything.
3. The request-response cycle
Every client-server interaction, no matter how complicated the system gets, boils down to this cycle: the client sends a request, the server processes it, the server sends back a response.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396262053-168005416.png
blocks.alt: A browser sending a request, the server processing it, and a response returning to the browser

blocks.content: 3.1 Anatomy of a request and a response
blocks.text: 3.1 Anatomy of a request and a response

blocks.content: A request typically says what you want and where to send it. A response says what happened and hands back whatever data was asked for.

["A request usually carries a method, a target address, some headers, and sometimes a body","A response carries a status code, some headers, and usually a body with the actual data","The client always sends first. The server never speaks unless it's been asked something"]
items: A request usually carries a method, a target address, some headers, and sometimes a body
A response carries a status code, some headers, and usually a body with the actual data
The client always sends first. The server never speaks unless it's been asked something

blocks.content: 3.2 A quick example over HTTP
Here's what that looks like on the wire when a client asks a server for a specific user.

curl -X GET https://api.example.com/users/42

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"id": 42, "name": "Asha"}

code.content:
curl -X GET https://api.example.com/users/42

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"id": 42, "name": "Asha"}

codes.text:
curl -X GET https://api.example.com/users/42

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"id": 42, "name": "Asha"}

blocks.title: Request response is synchronous by default
blocks.content: The client typically blocks and waits for the reply. Later in this course you'll see patterns, queues and websockets among them, that break out of this strict back and forth.
4. Thin clients versus thick clients
Not every client does the same amount of work. Where you draw the line between what the client handles and what the server handles is a real design decision, and it comes with trade-offs.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396262054-499945135.png
blocks.alt: A thin client relying on the server for almost everything, next to a thick client where the server does less

blocks.content: 4.1 Thin clients

A thin client does as little as possible on its own. It mostly displays what the server sends it and forwards whatever the user does back to the server. An old school terminal talking to a mainframe is the classic example, and a lot of modern web apps that render everything server side aren't far off.
4.2 Thick clients

A thick client holds more logic locally. It can validate input, render complex interfaces, even work with cached data while offline, and only talks to the server when it actually needs data or has to save something. Most modern mobile apps and single page web apps lean this way.
4.3 Making the trade-off

{"headers":["Pros","Cons"],"rows":[["Easy to build and update, most logic lives on the server","Useless without a network connection to the server"],["Works the same across almost any device","Every interaction round trips to the server, adding latency"],["Server can push fixes and features without updating the client","Server carries the entire compute and rendering burden"]]}

That table describes a thin client. A thick client flips most of these. It does more work locally, so it can feel faster and survive a flaky connection, but now you're shipping logic to every device, updating it separately across app stores, and duplicating some of what the server already knows how to do.
5. Stateless versus stateful servers, briefly

One more decision hides inside every server: does it remember you between requests, or does it treat every single request like it's coming from a stranger? This deserves its own deep dive later in the course, but it's worth knowing it exists here.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396262054-429341939.png
blocks.alt: Client requests hitting a stateful server that keeps session memory, versus a stateless server that keeps nothing

blocks.content: A stateful server keeps something about you in memory between requests, your login session or your shopping cart, whatever it needs to remember. A stateless server keeps nothing. Every request has to carry everything it needs to be understood on its own.

blocks.title: This gets its own dedicated topic
blocks.content: Statelessness is one of the most important properties in system design, worth a full topic on its own. For now, just know a server can either remember you between requests or treat every request like it's from a stranger.
6. The same pattern, everywhere you look
blocks.text: 6. The same pattern, everywhere you look

blocks.content: Once you know what to look for, client-server shows up under almost every technology you touch.
6.1 A browser and a web server
blocks.text: 6.1 A browser and a web server

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396262055-401958520.png
blocks.alt: A browser requesting a page from a web server, which pulls data from a database before responding

blocks.content: Your browser is the client. It sends a request for a page, the web server figures out what to send back, maybe pulling data from a database first, and hands over HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the browser to render.
6.2 A mobile app and a backend API
blocks.text: 6.2 A mobile app and a backend API

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396262055-433956312.png
blocks.alt: A mobile app requesting data from a backend API, which reads from its own database

blocks.content: Your phone's app is the client. It talks to a backend API over the internet, asking for your feed, your messages, or your account details, and the backend figures out the actual answer, often by talking to its own database.
6.3 A database client and a database server
blocks.text: 6.3 A database client and a database server

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396262056-963125705.png
blocks.alt: Application code acting as a database client, sending queries to a database server and receiving rows back

blocks.content: Even inside your own backend, this pattern repeats. Your application code is a database client, it sends a query, and the database server is what actually stores the data, runs the query, and sends rows back. Client-server, all the way down.
7. Where this pattern starts to strain
blocks.text: 7. Where this pattern starts to strain

blocks.content: The pattern is simple and it works beautifully, right up until one server has to answer everyone at once.
7.1 One server, too many clients
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396265432-618706230.png
blocks.alt: Four clients all sending requests to a single server that becomes overloaded

blocks.content: A single server has a limit, on CPU, on memory, on how many connections it can hold open at the same time. Add enough clients, and requests start queueing up, responses get slower, and eventually the server starts failing outright. The pattern that made everything so simple, one place to ask, becomes the exact thing holding you back.
7.2 What this motivates
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396265433-366363669.png
blocks.alt: The client server pattern branching into load balancing, horizontal scaling, and caching

blocks.content: This single limitation is the reason the rest of system design exists. Once one server can't keep up, you need ways to spread the work around without breaking the simple client-server contract clients already rely on.

["Load balancing, spreading requests across many servers instead of one","Horizontal scaling, adding more server instances as demand grows","Caching, answering repeat requests without redoing the same work","Stateless services, so any server in the fleet can handle any client's request"]
items: Load balancing, spreading requests across many servers instead of one
Horizontal scaling, adding more server instances as demand grows
Caching, answering repeat requests without redoing the same work
Stateless services, so any server in the fleet can handle any client's request

blocks.content: 8. Worked example: a todo app client and server
blocks.text: 8. Worked example: a todo app client and server

blocks.content: Let's make this concrete with the smallest possible real example, a todo app.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396265434-940322542.png
blocks.alt: A todo app client requesting a list of todos from a REST API server backed by a todos database

blocks.content: 8.1 The client side
The client is whatever renders your todo list, a web page or a mobile screen. When it loads, it asks the server for your current todos, and when you add one, it sends that new todo along.
8.2 The server side
The server exposes a couple of REST endpoints. It doesn't care whether the request came from a web page, a mobile app, or someone testing with curl, it just responds correctly to whatever asks.

blocks.title: Notice how little the client had to know
blocks.content: The client never touched a database, never wrote a query, never knew whether the todos lived in Postgres or MongoDB. It just asked, and the server did the actual work.
9. The interview angle
Client-server is so foundational that it's easy to skip past it in an interview and jump straight to fancier concepts. Don't. Naming it explicitly is worth more than it sounds like.
9.1 It's the starting assumption behind almost everything
blocks.text: 9.1 It's the starting assumption behind almost everything

blocks.content: Nearly every system design question, design a URL shortener, design a chat app, design an e-commerce checkout, assumes a client-server split before anything else gets decided. Saying so out loud shows you're building on solid ground, not skipping a step.
9.2 What's worth saying out loud

["Naming which part is the client and which part is the server before diving into design","Being explicit about what the request and response look like at each hop","Pointing out early where a single server would become a bottleneck","Using this pattern as the baseline, then layering caching, load balancing, and scaling on top of it"]
items: Naming which part is the client and which part is the server before diving into design
Being explicit about what the request and response look like at each hop
Pointing out early where a single server would become a bottleneck
Using this pattern as the baseline, then layering caching, load balancing, and scaling on top of it

blocks.content: 10. Summary

Client-server architecture splits every system into two roles: something that asks, and something that answers. That separation keeps clients thin, lets servers scale and improve independently, and lets one server's worth of logic and data serve any number of clients at once. It works well until a single server can't keep up, and that exact limit is what the rest of this course spends its time solving.
Almost every system you'll ever design starts with the same two boxes: something that asks, and something that answers. Everything else is just detail on top of that.
